source.title: InterPLM: Discovering Interpretable Features in Protein Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares neuron-level and SAE-feature representations in a protein language model, extending evidence about superposition and dictionary features to a new model domain.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports feature steering, but that result measures an intervention effect rather than whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical, or one-dimensional units. Amino-acid-type associations in randomized models are not evidence for the biological-concept result.
record.test_reason: The study trains SAEs on ESM-2-8M protein language model embeddings and compares SAE features with raw neurons on Swiss-Prot concept alignment. The authors present this as evidence of superposition in a new kind of real model, which bears on V4. It does not test the toy-model geometry, the capacity account, or the status of SAE features as units.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that the 46 vs 2,548 per-layer gap is strong evidence that PLMs store concepts in superposition, and that meaningful features require learned weights. They note that random-model SAEs still find amino-acid features and that their metrics only approximate biological interpretability.
record.recipe_differences: The original source studies sparse-feature superposition and its geometry in toy networks. This paper trains SAEs on ESM-2-8M embeddings and evaluates associations with Swiss-Prot annotations and neurons; it does not reproduce the toy-model method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported concept associations depend on the selected SAE model and the Swiss-Prot annotation and F1-threshold evaluation procedure; no comparison of these choices for the main neuron-versus-feature result is reported.

fits_no_version.finding: Clamping periodic-glycine SAE features on one position raises P(glycine) at masked periodic positions, whereas glycine-specific features affect only the steered position.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features in PLMs have causal, interpretable steering effects beyond the intervened token.

record.problems: The claim-relevant comparison is limited to ESM-2-8M and associations with available Swiss-Prot concepts; the paper says these metrics approximate biological interpretability. It does not establish feature completeness, stability, or canonical status. No uncertainty estimates are given for the reported neuron-versus-SAE counts.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results omitted. The paper's feature-steering results measure effects of interventions and do not test any listed claim version.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep, phase transition, or geometry analysis.
No test of capacity competition or of importance determining dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No test of alternative origins of polysemanticity.
Only ESM-2-8M (protein, 8M parameters); no text LLMs or larger models. No direct neuron-polysemanticity measurement beyond concept F1.
No completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, or canonicality tests. Fewer than 20% of features match any Swiss-Prot concept.
No comparison of 1-D with multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Randomized-weight SAEs yield hundreds of features strongly associated with individual amino-acid types (percent per layer).
Per-concept held-out F1 of the best feature versus the best neuron versus the random-model SAE.
Percent of SAE features per layer associated with any concept (under 20%).

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Counts are raw and unnormalized: 320 neurons versus 10,240 features per layer. The SAE per layer was selected by the same Swiss-Prot concept metric used for evaluation, which may inflate SAE counts relative to neurons. The neuron baseline used no such selection. Single small model; preprint.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-sparsity sweep, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry are tested.
The study does not test competition for limited representational capacity or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
It does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity alone is evidence of superposition.
Tests ESM-2-8M protein representations and Swiss-Prot concept alignment, not other language models or general-text LLMs.
Does not assess whether SAE features are complete, stable across training or settings, or canonical units.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional feature representations.

conditions.value: six layers; reported maximum per layer

rows.measure: Number of features with strong concept alignment
rows.baseline: ESM-2 neurons: up to 46 per layer
rows.note: The paper describes these as features with strong concept alignment; the figure caption specifies F1 > 0.5 in both validation and held-out sets.
rows.check: Raw counts compare a 10,240-feature dictionary with 320 neurons; per-unit percentages appear only in Fig 9a. No uncertainty is given, and the value reflects one selected SAE per layer.

rows.note: A direct representation comparator; the paper reports fewer clear concept associations for neurons than for SAE features.
rows.check: Neuron comparator. Few concept-aligned neurons (≤46 per layer of 320) is the V4-expected contrast, not a partial effect, so 'partial' is misleading. The count is not normalized against the 10,240 SAE features per layer.

rows.operation_detail: Measured Swiss-Prot biological-concept associations after shuffling model weights and training SAEs on the resulting embeddings.

conditions.value: shuffled within each weight and bias
same concept-based model selection and metric calculation process

rows.measure: Number of SAE features corresponding to biological Swiss-Prot concepts
rows.baseline: Learned ESM-2 weights: up to 2,548 features per layer with strong concept alignment
rows.value: Zero features corresponding to biological Swiss-Prot concepts
rows.note: The paper separately reports that randomized models had hundreds of features associated with individual amino-acid types.
rows.check: Control row: the absence is expected and strengthens R1–R4. The same randomized SAEs still yield hundreds of amino-acid-type features (Fig 9b); no row records this.

relationships.condition: ESM-2-8M protein LM, all six layers, learned weights
relationships.reason: SAE features align with far more Swiss-Prot concepts than neurons do (2,548 vs 46 per layer; 143 vs 15 concepts), and this vanishes with shuffled weights (R1–R5).
relationships.display_finding: SAE features aligned with far more Swiss-Prot concepts than neurons (2,548 vs 46 per layer; 143 vs 15 concepts), and the gap vanished with shuffled weights.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: ESM-2-8M protein LM, all six layers, learned weights
source_check.reason: R1–R4 report dictionary features associated with substantially more biological concepts than neurons; R5 supplies a randomized-weight control. These are indirect evidence consistent with V4 in this setting.

relationships.reason: Per the text (Fig 9b, not in rows), SAEs on random-weight models still recover hundreds of amino-acid features. So SAE-recoverable features partly reflect the data, not only the model (R5 context).
relationships.display_finding: SAEs trained on random-weight models still recovered hundreds of amino-acid features, so some SAE-recoverable features reflect the input data rather than only the trained model.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: The amino-acid associations reported in §3.3 and Figure 9b show that SAE interpretability can reflect input properties. V4 does not assert that all recoverable features require learned weights, so this finding does not establish a condition where V4 needs qualifying.

relation.reason: Its own annotation-alignment results bear on V4, beyond using SAEs as a tool.

tranche.reason: The study tests dictionary-recoverable representations in a new setting, protein language models, with neuron and randomized-weight comparisons.

source_check.notes: Counts compare 320 neurons with 10,240 dictionary features according to Methods §5.1.2; §3.1 inconsistently prints 10,420. Randomized-model amino-acid recovery is reported in §3.3/Figure 9b but has no dedicated result row.

statements.correction: Randomized ESM-2-8M SAEs: zero biological Swiss-Prot-concept features; hundreds of amino-acid-type-associated features. Methodological caveat about learned-representation specificity; no demonstrated failure of V4.
statements.problem: The ESM-2 findings are accurately reported, but their classification as limits_scope for V4 is unsupported: random-model amino-acid recovery qualifies the specificity of the evidence, without showing V4 failing or incomplete.
